props.title: Cruising

sections.content: Cruising ignited massive controversy upon release for its dark exploration of New York's underground gay leather scene through the lens of a police investigation. Director William Friedkin, fresh off successes with The Exorcist (1973) and The French Connection (1971), crafted a psychological thriller that blurred lines between observer and observed. Al Pacino delivers a haunting performance as Officer Steve Burns, who goes undercover to catch a killer targeting gay men. The film's explicit scenes and ambiguous ending sparked protests from LGBTQ+ activists who feared it would promote homophobia, while others defended its raw portrayal of a subculture rarely depicted in mainstream cinema.

sections.content: Friedkin's direction creates a suffocating atmosphere of paranoia and sexual tension, influenced by films like Taxi Driver (1976) and Looking for Mr. Goodbar (1977). The movie's technical achievements are notable - the nightclub scenes were filmed in actual leather bars with real patrons as extras, lending documentary-like authenticity. Cinematographer James Contner's work captures the neon-lit underworld with a gritty, voyeuristic style that would influence later films like Shame (2011) and Interior. Leather Bar (2013).

The film's legacy remains complex. While problematic in its portrayal of gay culture, Cruising broke new ground in depicting previously taboo subjects in mainstream cinema. Its influence can be seen in later LGBTQ+ themed crime films like The Silence of the Lambs (1991) and Mysterious Skin (2004). The ambiguous ending - leaving viewers uncertain about Burns' sexuality and the killer's true identity - reflects broader themes about identity and repression that still resonate. sections.content: Cruising marked a turning point in New Hollywood's treatment of LGBTQ+ themes. While earlier films like The Boys in the Band (1970) approached gay characters through a more theatrical lens, Friedkin's film merged exploitation elements with serious dramatic ambitions. This paved the way for more nuanced explorations in films like My Own Private Idaho (1991) and Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001), though its controversial legacy complicated its influence on the emerging New Queer Cinema movement of the 1990s.
